title: The Cracked Sidewalk
author: Eddie Killian
summary: Eddie Killian builds an extended engineering metaphor — the deliberate contraction joints cut into sidewalks to control where concrete cracks — into a sustained argument about how well-run organizations should treat failure. His central move is distinguishing two kinds of cracks: those that appear under the deliberately weakened joint (evidence the builder correctly anticipated stress and gave it a place to go) and those that appear elsewhere on the slab (evidence something moved that the design didn't anticipate, which demands investigation rather than just patching). He extends this to organizations: mechanisms like independent inspection, escalation routes, and reviews where 'red is permitted to remain red long enough to be understood' function as an organization's contraction joints, and expecting an organization to eliminate all failure is 'roughly equivalent to specifying concrete that will never shrink.' The essay's sharpest critique targets how organizations typically respond to unexpected failure — a new procedure, more reporting, retraining, a removed manager — arguing these often just patch the visible crack ('poured filler into an instrument') without asking why the problem surfaced outside the channels built to catch it. Killian's closing reframe is that visible cracks aren't a sign of dysfunction to be smoothed over; read correctly, they're a record — of what the design expected, and of what actually happened — and the gap between those two is where real organizational learning begins.
points: The core engineering fact reframed as organizational principle: 'maximum strength at every individual point is not the same thing as resilience of the whole' — deliberately weakening one place (a contraction joint, an escalation channel) can protect the larger structure rather than threaten it.

Killian's distinction between a crack under the joint (expected, evidence of good design) and a crack elsewhere on the slab (unexpected, evidence something moved outside the model) gives leaders a way to triage which failures need investigation versus which are functioning as designed.

His critique of typical organizational failure-response — 'a quality failure produces a new procedure... the visible opening disappears... sometimes someone has simply poured filler into an instrument' — targets the common leadership mistake of patching the symptom visible from the top rather than investigating why it surfaced there.

The diagnostic questions he proposes ('if reporting channels existed, why did the information travel around them? If people were authorized to raise concerns, why did they wait?') give leaders a specific line of inquiry when a problem appears outside the mechanisms built to catch it.
quotes: Concrete is extraordinarily strong in compression and comparatively weak in tension. A great deal of craft goes into influencing the outcome. Each decision reduces uncertainty. None repeals physics.

When tensile stress eventually exceeds what the concrete can accommodate, the slab cracks. If the joint has done its work, the fracture forms beneath the groove, where the irregular break is concealed within a straight, deliberately placed line. What looks like decoration is, in part, managed fracture.
Yet engineering does this routinely because maximum strength at every individual point is not the same thing as resilience of the whole.
A sufficiently well-managed organization is sometimes expected to eliminate such conditions. That expectation is roughly equivalent to specifying concrete that will never shrink.

A quality failure produces a new procedure. A missed target produces another reporting requirement. An accident produces retraining. The visible opening disappears. Sometimes the repair is correct. Sometimes someone has simply poured filler into an instrument.

If reporting channels existed, why did the information travel around them? If inspections existed, why was the defect discovered elsewhere? If people were authorized to raise concerns, why did they wait?
The contraction joints record what the designer expected. The cracks record what actually happened. The distance between those two is where the interesting work begins.
